title: Controlling mosquitoes with semiochemicals: a review

subsections.subsection_title: Ecological and Evolutionary Context of Mosquito Olfaction
subsections.content:
Mosquitoes transmit serious infectious diseases that include dengue, chikungunya, Rift Valley fever and malaria. In Africa, malaria remains as one of the most serious vector-borne diseases ref [1]. Malaria is spread by anopheline mosquitoes that transmit malaria parasites to humans. Of the hundreds of Anopheles species found worldwide, only a few dozen mediate the transmission of the Plasmodium parasite to humans ref [2]. Africa has over 128 native Anopheles mosquito species ref [1], with An. gambiae (sensu stricto), An. coluzzii and An. funestus being the predominant malaria vector species ref [1]. However, some minor species are also cause for concern. For example, the Asian native mosquito An. stephensi is now established in Ethiopia ref [1] and An. arabiensis is deemed a major cause of residual malaria transmission due to the species' insecticide avoidance behaviours ref [2].

Chemical cues and signals are used by both male and female mosquitoes to find a conspecific mating partner. This behaviour is crucial for mosquito reproductive success rates ref [11]. Differences exist between species regarding the type of chemical compounds that they use. In some species, females need to locate male swarms and they do this by using olfactory cues and perhaps the same visual cues that guide male mosquitoes to form swarms ref [20]. While in other species males find foraging females by following kairomones, chemicals involved in mosquito-host interactions, that are indicative of the presence of a female during her blood-feeding behaviour ref [11, ref [20]]. During this process, female mosquitoes are first attracted to a host, be it animal or human, through the kairomones that the host produces in breath, sweat or skin emanations ref [14]. Male mosquitoes, of certain species, then locate blood-feeding females by following the Fig. 1 An overview of the key behavioural patterns, influenced by semiochemicals, discussed in this review. The four main behaviours that are targeted include mating, oviposition, host-seeking and sugar feeding kairomone trail ref [11, ref [14]]. The behaviour of a male mosquito intercepting a female near a host is known to occur for Aedes spp. and Mansonia spp. of the Culicidae ref [11].

Takken ref [18] described the host-seeking behaviour of blood-feeding arthropods as "the orientation to a host from a distance". Host-seeking generally involves a series of behavioural steps that starts when the insect is activated by a host stimulus and ends when the mosquito lands on a suitable feeding area on the host ref [18]. Different behavioural cues are used during host-seeking and includes visual cues, long distance chemical stimulants (such as CO2, that activates and induces upwind flight), heat and moisture cues that play an important role in behavioural responses in close vicinity of the host, and skin odour cues that influence landing and biting site selection ref [18, ref [61], ref [62], ref [63]]. Semiochemical cues used in the host-seeking process are discussed in this section. Emphasis is placed on the importance of carbon dioxide in host finding, the use of host skin volatiles in host selection and/or preference, and lastly the effect of compound blends on host preference.

subsections.subsection_title: Chemical Cues in Mosquito Host Seeking
subsections.content:
Parasites & Vectors *Correspondence: marc.bouwer@fabi.up.ac.za feed at night. Changes in mosquito host preferences, time of feeding and an increase in outdoor feeding due to plasticity in mosquito behavioural responses have prompted the need for new and more environmentally friendly and robust vector control strategies that supplement current control strategies ref [5, 8]. The development and incorporation of novel vector control tools based on new scientific knowledge about mosquito behaviour and chemical ecology into integrated vector management (IVM) programmes are needed in order to reduce the burden and threat of mosquito-borne diseases ref [6].

It is proposed that both male and female mosquitoes produce aggregation pheromones that attract both sexes to the mating swarm ref [24]. How females locate male swarms is still unclear. Females may use similar visual cues (i.e. swarm markers) as males and olfactory cues, such as aggregation pheromones, to locate swarms ref [11, 20]. Laboratory studies have shown that when swarming Ae. aegypti males or females are placed upwind in an olfactometer a flight response is elicited in female mosquitoes, suggesting that both female and male Ae. aegypti produce a volatile attractant as one of many signals to initiate swarm formation ref [14, 24, 25]. Fawaz et al. ref [26] have identified 2,6,6-trimethylcyclohex-2-ene-1,4-dione (ketoisophorone), 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexane-1,4-dione (the saturated analogue of ketoisophorone) and 1-(4-ethylphenyl) ethanone as aggregation pheromones for Ae. aegypti. These compounds may be the same or structurally related to aggregation pheromones that related mosquito species use and should be evaluated further.

Kairomones play a key role in locating vital energy sources for flight and other metabolic activities in mosquitoes ref [11, 94]. Male mosquitoes feed exclusively on carbohydrate sources. In certain mosquito species, the female mosquitoes will take a sugar meal prior to bloodfeeding, whilst in other species the female will take a sugar meal after the blood meal ref [11, 94]. Here we review recent literature on how mosquitoes find these sugar meals with the focus on olfactory cues.

subsections.subsection_title: Sex and Mating Behavior Mediated by Semiochemicals
subsections.content:
Chemical cues and signals mediate key behaviours during the different stages in the life-cycle of an adult mosquito ref [1, 2]. Signals are produced for the specific purpose of changing the behaviour of an individual of a species, whereas cues are not produced for any specific purpose, but they are detected by individuals and can lead to behavioural responses ref [1]. Host finding by the adult mosquito occurs through a series of behavioural steps that are influenced by external chemical cues. A mosquito can be primed for activity by a specific chemical or blend produced by a potential host. This is followed by the initiation of flight to bring the insect within the vicinity of the source ref [18]. The mosquito will then continue to respond to external stimuli during flight for orientation through optomotor anemotaxis (movement in response to air currents and visual stimuli). Visual cues, such as contours against a background, that aid the mosquito during upwind flight and physical cues, such as convection heat and body moisture, play a role during host seeking. These cues, together with chemical cues, influence the orientation of a mosquito towards the host and can induce a landing response ref [11, 12, 18]. The individual importance of chemical, visual and physical cues that impact on the mosquito's flight behaviour is well studied. However, the mechanism of how these cues work together to result in specific types of behaviours remains a topic that requires further investigation.

The use of contact sex pheromones in dipterans for species recognition during mating is well documented, leading to the assumption that this mode of species recognition is also utilised by mosquitoes ref [2, 6]. Observations in support of sex pheromones for mosquitoes include studies done on adult male crabhole mosquitoes (Deinocerites cancer) ref [27] and winter mosquitoes (Culiseta inornata) ref [28] that revealed the male's ability to locate female pupae to mate with newly emerged virgin female mosquitoes ref [27]. Mating has also been perceived between males and empty pupal cases or recently dead females for winter and crabhole mosquito species ref [27, 28]. Culiseta inornata males have been observed touching conspecific mates with their front leg tarsi ref [28]. Furthermore, a decrease in mating attempts in Ae. albopictus males have been recorded when their terminal tarsomeres of the prothoracic and mesothoracic tarsi were treated with a solvent mixture ref [2, 29]. These studies found that short-range contact pheromones are most probably used by male and female mosquitoes in a swarm to recognise their own species. The volatility of aggregation pheromones makes these unlikely candidates for close range species recognition inside the swarm. This is due to the dynamic nature of swarms, specifically mixed species swarms ref [3, 4].

subsections.subsection_title: Challenges and Opportunities for Semiochemical-Based Control
subsections.content:

The selection of an oviposition site for many mosquito species is determined by visual and chemical cues ref [11]. Chemical cues, produced by conspecifics, used as oviposition attractants include egg raft, larval and pupal pheromones ref [11, 36]. The presence of conspecific larvae and their associated semiochemicals at oviposition sites indicates suitable conditions for larval development ref [36]. Breakdown products, in natural water bodies, of bacterial origin are also used as chemical cues for oviposition ref [11]. The chemical ecology and oviposition behaviour of gravid mosquitoes, including attractants and deterrents such as water salinity, phytochemicals and insecticides, was comprehensively reviewed by Bentley and Day ref [37]. An updated list and further research on oviposition attractants for mosquito larvae control is needed as targeting mosquito larvae is deemed a more successful long-term approach to vector control. Targeting larvae removes vectors before they can reproduce and transmit diseases ref [38]. This section highlights the influence of semiochemicals, singular or blends of chemical compounds, on oviposition site selection as well as egg-laying behaviour in mosquitoes.

Semiochemicals are known to be involved in the mating behaviour of mosquitoes. There are different behavioural patterns that occur at different mating stages and these also vary for different species ref [11, 20]. Mating behaviour includes maturation feeding (feeding required for an insect's gonads to mature for gamete production) followed by swarm formation, in some species, and a sequence of mate-finding behaviours that are guided by a set of chemical mating cues and signals ref [11]. Mating cues and signals are important to ensure the survival of a species and these cues and signals may help isolate a species, especially if they are unique to that species. Different, but related species that co-occur in the same environment sometimes have very similar odour cues and signals and, in such cases, isolation occurs by having mating period at different times of the day ref [21, 22]. This mechanism serves to prevent interspecies hybridisation ref [11]. Volatile chemicals that form part of the signals and cues used during these behaviours are thus not the same for the different species and need to be studied separately if specific control applications are to be developed. In this section a concise review of current insights into mate finding, swarm formation and mating cues with the emphasis on semiochemicals will be discussed.

Reviews by Navarro-Silva et al. ref [39] and Afify and Galizia ref [40] highlight the importance of semiochemicals that mediate oviposition in mosquitoes. Odour attractants involved in oviposition site selection have been identified from plant material, faeces from mosquito larvae as well as secretions from mosquito larvae, pupae and eggs ref [41, 42]. The first breakthrough on the use of chemical cues for oviposition site selection was with the identification of the oviposition pheromone, erythro-6-acetoxy-5-hexadecanolide, which was extracted from the apical droplet at the tip of the eggs of Cx. quinquefasciatus by Laurence and Pickett ref [43, 44]. Studies reviewed by Takken and Knols ref [11] have shown that gravid conspecifics, as well as Cx. tarsalis, are highly attracted to the erythro-6-acetoxy-5-hexadecanolide, and electrophysiological activity has also been demonstrated by Cx. quinquefasciatus in response to this pheromone ref [45]. Another major development on oviposition odour attractants was achieved by Lindh et al. ref [46] during a study conducted in Kenya which identified the first oviposition attractant for gravid female An. gambiae, namely cedrol. A follow-up study, conducted by Eneh et al. ref [47], on the natural source of the chemical, found that cedrol is produced by fungal species found on grass rhizomes near the natural mosquito breeding site. This brought to light the influence of both microbes and vegetation for oviposition site selection in mosquitoes.

subsections.subsection_title: Pathogen-Induced Changes in Host Odor and Mosquito Attraction
subsections.content: Skin volatiles play an important part in host preference for those mosquito species that are specialists on selected hosts ref [19]. Human skin volatiles have been studied intensively and over 500 compounds have been identified from human skin secretions ref [73, 74]. Variation in attractiveness between different individuals has been attributed to differences in skin-odour profiles as well as differences in human skin microbial flora ref [9, 11, 75]. The Knols group provided the first evidence of attraction of highly anthropophilic mosquitoes to a non-human odour source with experiments conducted on Limburger cheese. The smell of Limburger cheese is similar to sweaty human feet. This unique odour was traced back to the coryneform cheese bacteria, Staphylococcus epidermidis, that belong to the same genus as the coryneform bacteria found between the toes of human feet. Traps baited with Limburger cheese caught significantly more An. gambiae (s.s.) than the control traps ref [11, 76, 77]. A large amount of research has been done since the Limburger cheese experiments confirming the effect of chemical signals derived from skin microorganisms on the host-seeking behaviour in mosquitoes ref [78]. Malaria infection has been shown to alter host odor profiles, increasing attractiveness to mosquitoes through the release of specific metabolites such as (E)-4-hydroxy-3-methyl-but-2-enyl pyrophosphate, which triggers enhanced emission of CO₂, aldehydes, and monoterpenes from human red blood cells ref [3]. Studies have further demonstrated that both symptomatic and asymptomatic malaria infections induce consistent and detectable changes in human skin volatiles, enabling machine learning models to identify infection status with high sensitivity, even in low-parasitemia cases ref [2]. These pathogen-induced modifications in host odor represent a key evolutionary strategy by which Plasmodium enhances its transmission potential ref [1].

subsections.subsection_title: Carbon Dioxide and Synergistic Odor Blends in Host Location
subsections.content:
The vast amount of skin-associated volatiles makes bioassays aimed at determining the behavioural responses of mosquitoes almost impossible. Fortunately, sophisticated analytical techniques are now being applied for elucidating the identity of both specific semiochemicals and potential semiochemical blends. Electroantennogram (EAG) recordings can be used to investigate the antennal responses of mosquitoes to blends of chemicals and single sensillum recording (SSR) studies can be used to identify specific neuron function and type ref [11]. Gas chromatography coupled to electroantennogram (GC-EAG) recordings can then be used to separate components of blends and investigate their individual electrophysiological activity ref [11]. Electroantennogram responses are generally measured from the excised head of a mosquito mounted between two glass capillaries containing a saline solution and gold or silver electrode wires. The grounded indifferent electrode is inserted into the back of the decapitated head whilst the recording electrode is connected to the clipped antenna ref [57, 58, 84, 85].

Carbon dioxide (CO₂) plays a critical role in long-range host location, inducing upwind flight in mosquitoes such as Aedes aegypti, but near-host orientation and landing are primarily governed by human skin odours, with CO₂ having little influence once the mosquito is in close proximity ref [1]. In contrast, CO₂ acts as a powerful synergist for human-derived volatile blends, significantly enhancing the attractiveness of three-component blends (e.g., ammonia, lactic acid, tetradecanoic acid) when combined with specific C4 volatiles such as 3-methyl-1-butanol or butan-1-amine, reversing inhibition to attraction in a manner unique among insects ref [2]. The formulation of effective synthetic blends for malaria vector control has been refined through systematic testing, demonstrating that 3-methyl-1-butanol significantly enhances attraction of Anopheles gambiae to basic blends under both laboratory and semi-field conditions, and that its efficacy is dependent on the presence of CO₂ ref [4, 5]. These findings underscore that the behavioral response to odor blends is not additive but context-dependent, with CO₂ serving as a necessary modulator for the activity of many kairomones ref [2, 4].

subsections.subsection_title: Influence of Skin Microbiota on Mosquito Attractiveness
subsections.content: It is not very likely that all skin volatile compounds, with over 500 described in the literature, are simultaneously involved in host-seeking, landing and probing by mosquitoes. Semiochemical cues are rather thought to be specific combinations of a subset of these volatiles. Specific chemical combinations can arise out of combining subsets of only the semiochemicals that occur in the profiles of hosts. For example, it is known that specific compound blends of human skin volatiles are more likely to affect anthropophilic mosquito species such as Ae. aegypti and An. gambiae ref [5]. This finding can be rationalised because mosquitoes with different host preferences are more likely to respond to specific blends of volatile compounds that are associated with their preferred hosts ref [36] ref [38].

subsections.subsection_title: Human Skin Volatiles as Primary Kairomones for Mosquito Host Seeking
subsections.content:
Sandholm and Price ref [95] identified the potential of plant volatiles for luring mosquitoes as early on as 1962. These authors observed that certain mosquito species were attracted to light-coloured flowers with distinct odours in the field ref [95]. Various studies have since been done on the odour mediated sugar source-seeking behaviour in mosquitoes (reviewed by Nyasembe and Torto ref [96]). These studies revealed that floral odours play an important role for both male and female mosquitoes during sugar feeding ref [14, 94]. In 1988, Healy and Jepson ref [97] demonstrated an upwind flight and landing response for An. arabiensis and Ae. aegypti to the inflorescences of Achillea millefolium and Leucanthemum vulgare, respectively, during wind tunnel experiments ref [96]ref [97]ref [98]. Male and female An. arabiensis mosquitoes responded to the inflorescence as well as pentane extracts of A. millefolium flowers. A cyclic or bicyclic monoterpene was tentatively identified as the potential active component from these flowers ref [97].

Human skin volatiles serve as primary kairomones for mosquito host seeking, with numerous studies identifying key compounds emitted from different body regions. The chemical profile of skin volatiles varies significantly among individuals and body parts, with axillae, hands, and feet being the most frequently studied regions ref [1]. A comprehensive analysis of the human volatolome identified over 500 volatile organic compounds emanating from skin secretions, many of which are implicated in mosquito attraction ref [2]. Differential attractiveness of human foot odours to Anopheles gambiae sensu stricto has been demonstrated, with some individuals emitting odours up to 8-fold more attractive than others, linked to distinct chemical compositions ref [5]. Studies comparing volatiles from armpits, hands, and feet found that armpit emissions were initially less attractive due to deodorant residues, but when these were avoided, all body parts elicited comparable levels of attraction, confirming skin volatiles as the primary cue ref [6]. Electroantennogram and behavioural assays have shown that Anopheles gambiae sensu stricto exhibits selective sensitivity to human-specific sweat components, particularly (E)- and (Z)-3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid and 7-octenoic acid, with detection thresholds as low as 10⁻⁶ g ref [3]. Furthermore, synergistic interactions between ammonia, lactic acid, and carboxylic acids form a critical tripartite blend that guides host orientation, with the combination being significantly more attractive than any component alone ref [7].

subsections.subsection_title: Plant-Derived Semiochemicals in Mosquito Sugar Feeding and Behavior
subsections.content:
There is an urgent need to develop new odour-based traps to be used in IVM programmes in order to achieve the ambitious goals set out by the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the complete eradication of malaria goal set by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation ref [5]. To ensure the success of odour-based traps, the focus of lure development strategies using semiochemicals needs to shift to include other types of important vector species, such as An. arabiensis and An. funestus, as the majority of research to date, has been done on An. gambiae. Traps need to be able to target mosquito vectors during different life stages and key behaviours as well as target different sexes while being species-specific. Even though semiochemicals alone might not be adequate as a control tool against mosquitoes, using them in IVM programmes can provide a powerful tool that can help reduce and even eliminate vector populations. Odorants can be used to control mosquitoes by repelling, or by masking human odours, or by attracting mosquitoes with lures into traps. There are, however, substantial shortcomings with current attractants and repellents available to the public. N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET) for example requires high doses, is costly and has an unpleasant smell. Current commercial traps are expensive and bulky as they require a CO2 source and usually contain foul smelling synergists. Alternative traps made from recycled materials ref [108], such as buckets (for example the Gravid Aedes Trap) ref [109] and sticky traps, using products available in the home, such as castor oil ref [110], need further investigation as these can provide a low-cost and practical solution for vector control in developing countries. The focus of most of the research has primarily been on single olfactory compounds or blends containing less than five compounds. The effect of odour blends, synergistic or antagonistic, on mosquito host selection requires exploring, especially considering that more than 500 different chemicals are associated with human skin of which only a handful will be physiologically active in mosquitoes ref [65, 73, 74]. Mosquitoes rely on semiochemicals when searching for mates, oviposition sites, sugar meals and blood-hosts. These semiochemicals are potentially valuable for enhancing the selectivity and efficacy of odour-based traps and such traps can form an important part of the IVM strategy. The analytical challenge to find and identify these semiochemicals correctly should not be underestimated and the biologically active blend ratios need to be explored in much greater detail. Successful identification and formulation of these semiochemicals for control implementation will only come from a thorough understanding of the chemical ecology present in each mosquito species' life-cycle. Such knowledge will facilitate and guide future efforts in the search for these semiochemical cues and signals.

Plant-derived semiochemicals play a critical role in mosquito sugar feeding and behavior, with multiple studies demonstrating that both male and female mosquitoes rely on floral volatiles for energy acquisition ref [1, 5, 6, 7, 8]. For instance, Anopheles gambiae exhibits strong olfactory preferences for specific African plants such as S. didymobotrya and P. hysterophorus, whose volatile terpenoids drive upwind orientation in wind-tunnel assays ref [1]. Similarly, Anopheles arabiensis responds to long-range floral odours from Achillea millefolium, even in the absence of visual cues, indicating the potency of plant-derived semiochemicals in guiding nectar foraging ref [6]. The olfactory basis of mosquito-plant interactions extends beyond anophelines: Aedes aegypti is attracted to the nonanal-rich scent of Platanthera obtusata orchids, with neural responses in the antennal lobe mediating this preference ref [2]. Moreover, multimodal cues—including floral odorants, CO2, and visual signals from tansy inflorescences—synergistically enhance mosquito attraction beyond odor alone, suggesting that effective lures must integrate multiple sensory modalities ref [3]. Field-based studies further confirm that plant volatiles can be harnessed for vector control, as demonstrated by the development of ivermectin-based attractive toxic sugar baits (ATSBs) that exploit mosquito sugar-feeding behavior to deliver lethal doses to An. arabiensis ref [8]. Olfactory-based detection methods have also been applied in host plant forensics, enabling identification of plant species used by Afro-tropical malaria vectors in the wild, thereby informing lure design ref [4].

This preference is easily countermanded by internal physiological factors, such as the level of starvation, and by external factors such as host availability ref [11, 19]. If there is an urgent need to feed, then the mosquito may settle for hosts that are normally not preferred. The physiological state of the mosquito will thus influence its response to certain behavioural cues. This state varies depending on the age, size, nutritional status and gonotrophic stage of the mosquito. Once the optimal internal state for a specific reaction is met then the mosquito will respond in the appropriate manner to the correct stimulus ref [11]. This plasticity in mosquito behaviour can impede the identification of important mosquito semiochemicals because the species being studied needs to be in the correct state to respond. This adds to the analytical challenge of correctly identifying semiochemicals that mediate certain behaviours.

subsections.subsection_title: Oviposition Site Selection via Chemosensory Cues
subsections.content: Mosquitoes employ a sophisticated array of chemosensory cues to identify and select oviposition sites, ensuring offspring survival in environments conducive to larval development. Female mosquitoes detect volatile and non-volatile chemical signals emanating from microbial biofilms, decaying organic matter, and conspecific eggs, which collectively serve as indicators of habitat quality. Studies have demonstrated that specific carboxylic acids, such as isovaleric and propionic acid, act as potent attractants, while phenolic compounds and ammonia derivatives modulate site preference through dose-dependent effects. The integration of these cues is mediated by olfactory and gustatory receptors expressed in the antennae and tarsi, enabling spatial and temporal discrimination between suitable and unsuitable sites. Notably, the presence of conspecific eggs can trigger either attraction or repulsion, depending on species-specific thresholds and ecological context, suggesting an evolved balance between competition avoidance and kin recognition. Recent advances in electrophysiological and genetic analyses have begun to unravel the neural circuits underlying these behaviors, though the precise molecular identity of many receptor-ligand interactions remains unresolved. Understanding these chemosensory mechanisms offers promising avenues for the development of lure-and-kill strategies that exploit oviposition behavior to reduce vector populations. ref [1]

The sexual chemoecology of mosquitoes is governed by a complex array of reproductive semiochemicals that mediate mate recognition, courtship behavior, and copulation success. Male mosquitoes, particularly in species such as Anopheles and Aedes, rely heavily on auditory and chemical cues to locate and identify conspecific females, with female-emitted volatile organic compounds playing a pivotal role in long-range attraction and species-specific mating. Recent studies have identified key sex-specific hydrocarbons and esters that serve as pheromonal signals, enabling males to distinguish between conspecifics and heterospecifics, thereby reducing maladaptive mating attempts. In addition, the timing of pheromone release is tightly synchronized with swarming behavior, suggesting an evolutionary adaptation to maximize reproductive efficiency in ephemeral mating aggregations. The molecular identity of these semiochemicals remains incompletely characterized, but advances in gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and electrophysiological assays have begun to elucidate the chemical signatures underlying sexual communication. Understanding these mechanisms offers promising avenues for the development of semiochemical-based mating disruption strategies, such as synthetic lures that mimic female signals to trap or confuse males, thereby reducing population fecundity without chemical insecticides. Such approaches align with integrated vector management goals by targeting reproduction at the behavioral level, minimizing ecological disruption ref [1].

Phytochemicals, derived from a diverse array of plant species, have emerged as critical components in the chemical ecology of mosquito behavior. These volatile organic compounds, including terpenoids, phenylpropanoids, and aliphatic esters, are emitted by host plants and can act as attractants, repellents, or oviposition cues for mosquito vectors. For instance, certain monoterpenes such as limonene and linalool have been shown to disrupt host-seeking behavior in Aedes aegypti, while others like citronellal and eugenol elicit strong avoidance responses. Conversely, some phytochemicals, particularly those released by flowering plants or decaying vegetation, serve as kairomones that guide gravid females to suitable breeding sites. The ecological specificity of these interactions suggests that plant-mosquito semiochemical relationships are evolutionarily tuned, with variations observed across mosquito species and geographic populations. Recent studies have begun to elucidate the olfactory receptor mechanisms underlying phytochemical detection, revealing that mosquito antennae express distinct odorant-binding proteins that selectively respond to plant-derived volatiles. This growing body of evidence positions phytochemicals not merely as incidental environmental cues but as integral, modifiable elements in semiochemical-based vector control strategies. Further research is needed to standardize extraction protocols, quantify field-relevant concentrations, and assess long-term behavioral adaptation in mosquito populations exposed to synthetic analogs of these natural compounds.ref [1]

subsections.subsection_title: CO₂ in synthetic odor blends for trapping and surveillance
subsections.content: Carbon dioxide is the best-known mosquito kairomone and its role in mosquito host location has been intensively studied ref [20]. The gas is responsible for priming the flight response and guiding mosquitos to their hosts ref [51], ref [5]. Mosquitoes have been shown to respond to very small changes in atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (~ 0.035%) ref [20]. Host recognition through changes in CO₂ levels usually occurs over distances of approximately 10 m when the ambient CO₂ level changes by the addition of a breath plume containing ~ 4% CO₂ ref [51]. A source of CO₂ is often added to traps as an additional attractant. This can be done by adding dry ice, releasing CO₂ from gas canisters, or fermenting sugar and molasses in a trap to produce CO₂. Carbon dioxide substitutes such as 2-butanone can also be added to traps ref [5], ref [20].

subsections.subsection_title: Neurophysiological detection of CO₂ in mosquito host-finding
subsections.content:
Carbon dioxide is the best-known mosquito kairomone and its role in mosquito host location has been intensively studied ref [1]. The gas is responsible for priming the flight response and guiding mosquitos to their hosts ref [1]. Mosquitoes have been shown to respond to very small changes in atmospheric CO 2 concentrations (~ 0.035%) ref [1]. Host recognition through changes in CO 2 levels usually occurs over distances of approximately 10 m when the ambient CO 2 level changes by the addition of a breath plume containing ~ 4% CO 2 ref [1]. A source of CO 2 is often added to traps as an additional attractant. This can be done by adding dry ice, releasing CO 2 from gas canisters, or fermenting sugar and molasses in a trap to produce CO 2. Carbon dioxide substitutes such as 2-butanone can also be added to traps ref [1].

Carbon dioxide is a general cue indicative of the presence of a vertebrate host but mosquitoes do not only rely on CO 2 because it does not convey information on the potential suitability of the host ref [1]. There is also variation in how different mosquito species use and respond to CO 2. Some opportunistic mosquito species, such as An. arabiensis, feed on both humans and animals and use CO 2 as a general host cue whereas other species, such as An. gambiae, prefer humans and rely on CO 2 and other odours that are specific to humans to guide them during flight ref [1]. The generality of using CO 2 in hostseeking is thought to increase with the degree of zoophily in mosquito feeding behaviour ref [1]. Carbon dioxide, by itself, may not be suitable as a chemical lure for selectively trapping vector mosquitoes and in particular not for selectively trapping anthropophilic vector mosquitoes. However, CO 2 remains an important synergist of host specific chemical cues. Further field work is needed to improve the effectiveness and specificity of CO 2 as a lure.

Behavioural responses of mosquitoes do not only depend on the presence of CO 2. Carbon dioxide, human odour and heat was needed to elicit a robust feeding response in wild-type Ae. aegypti mosquitoes. The study, by Raji et al. ref [1] highlighted the importance of considering synergistic chemical compounds, as well as the interaction between chemical and physical cues when studying vector-host interactions. Removing either CO 2, heat or odour resulted in a reduced feeding response ref [1]. The intricate combination of both chemical and physical cues that mosquitoes rely on during vector-host interactions complicates the development of artificial lures. This is because chemical lures by themselves do not replicate the physical cues that may be required to elicit the desired behavioural response from the mosquito.

subsections.subsection_title: CO₂ as a primary flight activator and long-range attractant
subsections.content:
Carbon dioxide is the best-known mosquito kairomone and its role in mosquito host location has been intensively studied ref [11, 61]. The gas is responsible for priming the flight response and guiding mosquitos to their hosts ref [11, 19, 61, 66]. Mosquitoes have been shown to respond to very small changes in atmospheric CO 2 concentrations (~ 0.035%) ref [12, 67]. Host recognition through changes in CO 2 levels usually occurs over distances of approximately 10 m when the ambient CO 2 level changes by the addition of a breath plume containing ~ 4% CO 2 ref [12]. A source of CO 2 is often added to traps as an additional attractant. This can be done by adding dry ice, releasing CO 2 from gas canisters, or fermenting sugar and molasses in a trap to produce CO 2. Carbon dioxide substitutes such as 2-butanone can also be added to traps [66, ref [3]].

Carbon dioxide is a general cue indicative of the presence of a vertebrate host but mosquitoes do not only rely on CO 2 because it does not convey information on the potential suitability of the host ref [11, 19, 61]. There is also variation in how different mosquito species use and respond to CO 2. Some opportunistic mosquito species, such as An. arabiensis, feed on both humans and animals and use CO 2 as a general host cue whereas other species, such as An. gambiae, prefer humans and rely on CO 2 and other odours that are specific to humans to guide them during flight ref [19, 66]. The generality of using CO 2 in hostseeking is thought to increase with the degree of zoophily in mosquito feeding behaviour ref [61]. Carbon dioxide, by itself, may not be suitable as a chemical lure for selectively trapping vector mosquitoes and in particular not for selectively trapping anthropophilic vector mosquitoes. However, CO 2 remains an important synergist of host specific chemical cues. Further field work is needed to improve the effectiveness and specificity of CO 2 as a lure.

Behavioural responses of mosquitoes do not only depend on the presence of CO 2. Carbon dioxide, human odour and heat was needed to elicit a robust feeding response in wild-type Ae. aegypti mosquitoes. The study, by Raji et al. ref [72] highlighted the importance of considering synergistic chemical compounds, as well as the interaction between chemical and physical cues when studying vector-host interactions. Removing either CO 2, heat or odour resulted in a reduced feeding response ref [72]. The intricate combination of both chemical and physical cues that mosquitoes rely on during vector-host interactions complicates the development of artificial lures. This is because chemical lures by themselves do not replicate the physical cues that may be required to elicit the desired behavioural response from the mosquito.
